title: AHPI calls for trusted, interoperable and secure digital healthcare with strong AI governance at InnoHEALTH 2026

contentHtml:

The future of digital healthcare will depend not merely on technological innovation but on the ability to build a connected, secure, accountable and trustworthy healthcare ecosystem. Emphasising this need, the Association of Healthcare Providers (India) (AHPI) highlighted the importance of interoperability, responsible artificial intelligence (AI), data privacy and cybersecurity at InnoHEALTH 2026, held on 20–21 November 2026 at Jamia Millia Islamia University, New Delhi.

The conclave featured a panel discussion titled “Trusted Digital Health-Interoperability, AI Governance, and Cybersecurity”, bringing together experts from academia, clinical practice, healthcare leadership and the technology sector to deliberate on emerging opportunities, challenges and priorities in India’s rapidly evolving digital health landscape.

The session was moderated by Dr Sunil Kumar Khetarpal, Deputy Director General, AHPI, and featured Dr Amit Raj, Founder, Plexus AI; Surg Capt (Dr) Vijaya Kumar Bodasingu, Former Executive Director, KIMS Hospitals; Dr Anandhi Ramachandran, Professor, IIHMR Delhi; Dr Bhupinder Chaudhary, Associate Professor, Jamia Millia Islamia; and Abhishekk Kumar, CEO and Founder, ConsentAccess.

The deliberations focused on three critical pillars shaping the future of digital healthcare: seamless interoperability between healthcare information systems, responsible and accountable AI governance, and robust cybersecurity frameworks to safeguard sensitive health information.

The panellists emphasised that fragmented digital systems, inconsistent data standards and inadequate integration continue to pose challenges to seamless information exchange across healthcare institutions. The discussion also highlighted the need for responsible AI adoption, including appropriate validation, transparency, human oversight and clearly defined accountability mechanisms. With increasing digitisation of health records and clinical processes, data protection, patient consent and cybersecurity preparedness must become integral components of healthcare delivery.

The discussion reinforced that digital health solutions must go beyond technological sophistication to demonstrate clinical relevance, reliability, patient safety and measurable improvements in healthcare outcomes. Building public confidence will require healthcare providers, technology developers, policymakers and academic institutions to work together towards common standards and governance frameworks.

Speaking on the occasion, Dr Sunil Kumar Khetarpal, Deputy Director General, AHPI, said, “Digital transformation in healthcare must be guided by the needs of patients and the realities of clinical practice. Artificial intelligence and connected technologies offer enormous opportunities to improve the quality, accessibility and efficiency of healthcare delivery. However, their adoption must be supported by seamless interoperability, robust data protection, appropriate validation and clear accountability frameworks. Technology must complement clinical judgement rather than replace it. Ultimately, trust will determine the acceptance and sustainability of digital healthcare, and patient interests must remain at the centre of every technological advancement.”

The discussion also underscored the importance of strengthening collaboration between healthcare providers, technology companies, academia and policymakers to ensure that digital innovations translate into meaningful and sustainable improvements in healthcare delivery.

AHPI reiterated the importance of promoting a digital healthcare ecosystem that balances innovation with patient safety, data privacy, cybersecurity and responsible governance. Such an approach will be essential to building a connected, inclusive and trusted digital health ecosystem for India.
